title: The third week
hook: walking with Christ through the passion

segments.voice: Yesterday, the deathbed test: weigh a choice from the very end, and decide now as you'd wish you had then. Your line was from the end. Which small decision did you look at from there? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

It's late, in a garden on the Mount of Olives. The supper is over. Jesus takes three of his friends a little way apart from the others and asks them for one thing. Not to argue his case. Not to fight. Not to find a way out. Just to stay awake and stay near. Then he goes a short distance further, falls on his face, and prays. When he comes back, they're asleep. The third week of the Spiritual Exercises begins on nights like this one, and asks the person praying to do what those friends could not.
screen: `A GARDEN, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `JUST STAY NEAR.` → `THEY FELL ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: The third week walks with Christ through the passion: from the supper with his friends, through the garden, the arrest, the trials, the cross and the tomb. What's striking is what Ignatius asks the person to want. Not insight. Not a lesson. He tells them to ask for sorrow with Christ in sorrow, anguish with Christ in anguish. With. That's the word that matters. The first week looked at sin, and could feel like standing in the dock. This is different. It's companionship: staying beside someone who is suffering. Ignatius gives a few things to notice as the scenes pass. Notice what Christ suffers in his humanity. Notice how the divinity hides itself: he could stop it, and doesn't. And notice that he suffers this for me, and ask what I ought to do and to bear for him. He even suggests a kind of fast for the imagination. During this week, don't call up joyful thoughts, even good and holy ones like the resurrection. Stay in the scene. Don't skip ahead to Sunday. In the garden, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says to his three friends: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death: stay you here, and watch with me." Stay. Watch. With me. He didn't ask them to fix anything. And the Gospel is honest: they slept, more than once. The third week gives the one praying a second chance at that night. Away from prayer it can look like a plastic chair in a hospital hallway, a long phone call, a friend's kitchen after a funeral. Sometimes nobody can make the pain stop. Staying is still something.
screen: `FROM THE SUPPER TO THE TOMB.` · `SORROW WITH CHRIST IN SORROW.` · `THE DIVINITY HIDES ITSELF.` · `DON'T SKIP AHEAD TO SUNDAY.` · then, large: `STAY YOU HERE, AND WATCH WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk with him for the length of this sit. Settle, and breathe. Choose one scene: the garden at night, the road with the cross, or the foot of the cross. Put yourself there, quietly, a few steps behind. Don't try to say anything clever. Just stay. Notice the faces, the dust, the sounds. If you pray, you can ask, as Ignatius does, for sorrow with Christ in his sorrow. If you don't, you can bring to mind someone who is suffering right now and keep them company in your thoughts. The bell holds the time.
The third week. Walking with Christ through the passion, from the supper to the tomb, asking to stay beside him in his sorrow. Today's word.
Your line: suffer with. Today, when someone tells you something hard, resist the urge to fix it. Stay with them a minute longer than feels comfortable. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: In the third week of an Ignatian retreat, people contemplate the passion scene by scene, from the Last Supper to the burial, asking for the grace of sorrow with Christ in his sorrow.

sources.ref: Spiritual Exercises, third week (no. 190–209), especially no. 195–197, 203 and 206

notes: The outline practice is 'walk with him for five minutes'; the app's sit is two minutes, so the practice says 'for the length of this sit'.

Paraphrases: the grace of sorrow with Christ in sorrow (no. 203), the points on his humanity, the hidden divinity and 'for my sins' (nos. 195–197), and the addition about not bringing up joyful thoughts, even of the resurrection (no. 206). Confirm.
'They slept, more than once' follows Matthew 26:40–45; confirm. Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 26:38 and the Greek 'γρηγορεῖτε μετ' ἐμοῦ' to confirm.
